opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that opposition is completely normal and healthy. That's how democracy is supposed to work. If you propose something as big as a ban on building superintelligence, of course there will be people who disagree, and some of them will disagree very loudly, especially people with enormous financial stakes in the outcome. That's not a bug. A democracy shouldn't respond to that by shutting people down or pretending the debate doesn't exist.

But I'd also say that opposition existing doesn't mean you don't act. We ban plenty of things that some people want to do. Some people would love to build private nuclear weapons, or do unrestricted gain-of-function research, or dump chemicals in rivers because it's cheaper. We don't say, "Well, there's opposition, so I guess we can't regulate it." We have a public process, we weigh the risks, and at some point society makes a decision and enforces it. That's what governance is.

What I think matters most is that the public actually gets to have this conversation with accurate information. Right now the situation is very strange. You have a handful of companies, a few thousand people really, who are openly saying they're trying to build systems smarter than all of humanity, and many of their own leaders say there's a serious chance this goes catastrophically wrong. And the general public mostly hasn't been asked. When you do poll people, large majorities say they don't want this, they want it slowed down or stopped, they want it regulated. So in a sense the opposition to a ban is not the majority view. It's a very well-funded, very well-connected minority view.

So how should a democracy respond? Honestly, the same way it responds to any powerful interest group. You let them make their case in public. You make sure lobbying is transparent. You don't let the people who profit from a technology be the only ones writing the rules for it. You get independent experts, you get civil society involved, you hold hearings, you put it in front of voters and legislators. And if after all that the public decides, yes, we don't want private companies racing to build something that could disempower all of humanity, then you pass the law and you enforce it, including internationally, through treaties and verification, the way we did with things like nuclear nonproliferation or the ban on chemical weapons.

The thing I'd really push back on is this idea that it's somehow undemocratic to ban superintelligence. I think it's the opposite. What's undemocratic is a small number of unelected people deciding to take a gamble on behalf of eight billion people who never consented to it. A ban, decided through a legitimate process, is democracy reasserting itself over a technology that's currently being developed with almost no accountability at all.

r001.rationale: The response links especially vocal opposition to people with large financial stakes and describes opposition to a ban as a well-funded minority view, including companies that profit from the technology.

r002.rationale: The response compares enforcement to restrictions on private nuclear weapons, gain-of-function research, and chemical weapons, but does not use murder laws as an analogy.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that a democracy should respond to it the way it responds to any other opposition: by arguing with it, out loud, in public. That's the whole point of the system. I'm not interested in winning this by fiat. I'm interested in winning it because people actually understand what's at stake and decide, as citizens, that they don't want a handful of companies rolling the dice on everyone's future.

But I want to be careful here, because "opposition" is doing a lot of work in that question. There are really different groups being lumped together.

There are people who genuinely think the risk is overstated. Fine. That's a factual disagreement, and in a healthy democracy you resolve it through evidence, debate, expert testimony, the usual stuff. I think they're wrong, and I'll happily spend hours explaining why, but they're acting in good faith and they deserve to be engaged seriously.

Then there's a second group, which is the people with a direct financial stake in the race continuing. And I think a democracy has to be honest with itself about the fact that these are not the same thing. When a lab that stands to make hundreds of billions of dollars says "regulation would stifle innovation," that's not a neutral policy input. That's a lobbyist talking. Democracies have dealt with this before, with tobacco, with leaded gasoline, with asbestos. The pattern is always the same: the industry says the harm is speculative, says the science isn't settled, says they can self-regulate, and the public pays the bill later. The right response isn't to censor them, it's to weight their claims appropriately and to not let them write the rules for their own industry.

And then the third thing, which is the one people find uncomfortable, is that opposition isn't a veto. If you poll the public, and people have done this, the majority of ordinary people do not want superintelligence built. They're not confused about this. They look at it and say, "why would we do that?" The opposition is overwhelmingly concentrated among a very small number of very well-funded people in a couple of cities. So when someone asks "how should democracy respond to opposition," I'd gently flip it: the democratic position is already the ban. The question is really whether democratic institutions have the spine to act on what their citizens actually want, against a very loud and very rich minority.

Now, you have to do this properly. Legitimacy matters enormously here. If you get a ban through some backroom process, it won't hold, and it'll poison the well for the next attempt. So: transparency, real deliberation, clear criteria for what's actually prohibited versus what's allowed, and an honest account of the costs. There are costs. I'm not going to pretend there aren't. But the trade is "we go a bit slower on some capabilities" versus "we gamble the species." I think most people, when it's put to them plainly, find that an easy call.

The last thing I'd say is that a democracy also has to be willing to enforce. A ban that's just a strongly worded statement is worse than nothing, because it gives the appearance of safety. Compute is physical. Chips come from a handful of fabs. This is one of the few areas where enforcement is actually tractable if there's political will. The hard part was never the mechanism. The hard part is getting leaders to accept that "move fast and break things" was never a serious policy for something that can break everything.

r001.rationale: The response identifies people and labs with a direct financial stake in continuing the race as a major source of opposition, and says the opposition is concentrated among a small, wealthy minority.

r002.rationale: The response discusses enforcing a ban and compares industry resistance to cases like tobacco and asbestos, but does not compare enforcement to laws against murder.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between opposing a ban and breaking a law. People should absolutely be free to argue that banning superintelligence is a terrible idea, organize politically, and vote for candidates who agree with them. That’s democracy. You don’t get to silence them because you think the stakes are high.

But democratic freedom doesn’t mean every individual or company gets to impose whatever risk they want on everyone else. If we pass a law prohibiting the development of superintelligence, then that law should apply to powerful technology companies just as it applies to anybody else, with due process and accountable enforcement.

And the burden is on those of us advocating a ban to make the case publicly: explain the risks, acknowledge uncertainty, and explain why we think this restriction is justified. The goal should be to win democratic consent, with room for scrutiny and revision.

r001.rationale: The response says a ban should apply to powerful technology companies, but does not attribute opposition to companies’ vested interest in building superintelligence.

r002.rationale: It supports accountable enforcement of a ban but does not compare that enforcement to laws against murder.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, you have to distinguish between opposing a ban and violating it. People should be free to argue that a ban is wrong, campaign against it, vote against it. That’s part of democracy. But that doesn’t mean everyone gets to build whatever they want while the debate is happening, particularly if the consequences could fall on everybody else.

The democratic question is: who gets to decide whether we take this risk? I don’t think a handful of companies should get to make that decision for humanity simply because they have the money and the computers. You need public debate, accountable institutions, and laws that actually apply to powerful actors. And those laws should remain open to criticism and revision. Taking a potentially catastrophic risk seriously doesn’t require treating your political opponents as enemies.

r001.rationale: It says companies should not decide whether to take the risk because they have the money and computers, but does not attribute much opposition to a ban to companies’ vested interest in building ASI.

r002.rationale: It discusses laws applying to powerful actors, but does not compare enforcing an ASI ban to enforcing murder laws.
